title: Strat Chat: Circulation
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: Classroom circulation—how teachers move around the room during instruction and independent work—serves two distinct purposes: proximity-based behavior management and targeted scaffolding for students at their point of need. A teacher's physical presence is powerful enough that moving toward disruption often corrects off-task behavior without a word, though over-reliance on constant movement can itself become disruptive. The ideal approach builds such strong routines that behavior-management circulation is rarely needed, making each movement more impactful. For academic support, teachers should resist visiting students who are already succeeding and instead chart a deliberate path to those with the most need, providing verbal scaffolds so struggling learners can access the same level of work as their peers. Circulation also enables strategic cold-calling: sampling student thinking on mini-whiteboards during independent work allows teachers to plan precisely who gets asked which questions. Purposeful movement signals accountability and care, reinforcing the high expectations teachers have established for every student every lesson.
points: Teacher circulation serves two purposes: proximity-based behavior management and deliberate scaffolding for students at their point of need—and the best classrooms need little of the former.
The physical presence of a teacher is a behavior management tool on its own; mere movement toward disruption can correct off-task behavior without a word.
Over-circulation for behavior management can itself become disruptive; strong routines make each movement more powerful precisely because it is rare.
During independent work, teachers should move first to students with the greatest need—not the most confident students—and use circulation to sample thinking for strategic cold-calling.
quotes: As teachers we do not want to find ourselves bolted to our desks at the front of the room as this gives students additional opportunities to stop paying attention and display off-task behaviours.

The physical presence of a teacher is a powerful thing. It is amazing that the mere movement of a teacher towards the area of disruption or off-task behaviour can lead to a quick, positive change in behaviour without as much as a single word from the teacher.
Ideally, by building strong routines and high expectations of your class then the requirements for circulating to manage behaviour will actually be minimal.
The alternate and more ideal use of circulation is that once behaviour is settled you can begin to use circulation to help scaffold for students to meet them at their point of need.
Instead, the teacher should first conduct an exaggerated scan of the room and then move immediately to the students with the most need.
When we are not tethered to the front of the room it shows the students not only that they are accountable, but also that we greatly care about the progress which they are making.
